In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

**Surat Qaf**

It is also called Surat al-Basiqat. It is Meccan by consensus, and its verses number forty-five.

Ibn Kathir said: This surah is the first of the *hizb al-mufassal* (the section of the Qur'an comprising the short surahs, from *mufassal*, "well-differentiated," according to the sound view. It was also said that it begins with Surat al-Hujurat. As for what the common people say, that it is from *'amma* (Surat al-Naba'), there is no basis for it, and none of the reputable scholars said it, as far as we know. The evidence is what Aws ibn Hudhayfa narrated, that he said: I asked the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ how they divided the Qur'an into *ahzab* (sections, singular *hizb*)? They said: three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, and the *mufassal* section alone. So when you count forty-eight surahs, the one after them is Surat Qaf.

Its explanation:

Three: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, and al-Nisa'.

Five: al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, al-Anfal, and Bara'ah.

Seven: Yunus, Hud, Yusuf, al-Ra'd, Ibrahim, al-Hijr, and al-Nahl.

Nine: Subhan (al-Isra'), al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha, al-Anbiya', al-Hajj, al-Mu'minun, al-Nur, and al-Furqan.

Eleven: al-Shu'ara', al-Naml, al-Qasas, al-'Ankabut, al-Rum, Luqman, Alif-Lam-Mim al-Sajdah, Saba', Fatir, and Ya-Sin.

Thirteen: al-Saffat, Sad, al-Zumar, Ghafir, Ha-Mim al-Sajdah, Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf, al-Zukhruf, al-Dukhan, al-Jathiyah, al-Ahqaf, al-Qital, al-Fath, and al-Hujurat.

(p-5481) Then after that comes the *hizb al-mufassal*, as the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said. Thus it is established that its beginning is Surat Qaf.

The Imam Ahmad, Muslim, and the authors of the Sunan narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Abu Waqid al-Laythi: What did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite at the 'Eid? He said: "Qaf" and "al-Iqtarabat" (Surat al-Qamar).

Muslim and others narrated from Umm Hisham bint Haritha ibn al-Nu'man, who said: I did not memorize Surat Qaf except from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He used to deliver the sermon with it every Friday.

In another narration: He used to recite it every Friday on the pulpit when he addressed the people.

The purpose is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite this surah at the great gatherings, such as the 'Eid and the Friday prayers, because it includes the origin of creation, the resurrection, the rising, the return, the standing, the reckoning, Paradise and Hell, reward and punishment, and encouragement and warning. End.

(p-5482) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾

It is one of the letters of the disjointed letters (*huruf al-tahajji*) with which the surahs open, like Sad, Nun, Alif-Lam-Mim, Ha-Mim, and similar ones. It is a name for the surah, according to the sound opinion among the views, as has been mentioned repeatedly before.

A note:

Ibn Kathir said: It was narrated from some of the early scholars (*salaf*) that they said: "Qaf" is a mountain surrounding the whole earth, called the Mountain of Qaf.

It seems that this, and Allah knows best, is from the fables of the Children of Israel, which some people took from them, because they saw that narrating from them is permissible in matters that are neither confirmed nor denied. In my view, this and similar things are fabrications of some of their heretics, who confuse people about the matter of their religion, just as fabricated hadiths were attributed to the Prophet ﷺ in this Ummah, despite the high standing of its scholars, memorizers, and imams. And there is no time for one who comes first, so how about the Nation of the Children of Israel, with the long span of time, the scarcity of memorizers and critics among them, their drinking of wine, their scholars' distortion of words from their places, and their alteration of the books and verses of Allah?! The Lawgiver only permitted narrating from them in His saying: "Narrate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm," regarding what reason may permit. As for what reason rejects, and what is judged to be false, and where the probability of its falsehood prevails, it is not of this category.

Many of the early exegetes (*mufassirun*), and likewise a great number of later ones, have also narrated from the books of the People of the Book in interpreting the glorious Qur'an, though they have no need for their reports, and to Allah belongs all praise and favor.

(p-5483) Then Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected what was said, that the meaning of "Qaf" is "the matter has been decided, by Allah!" like the saying of the poet:

*I said to her, "Stop," and she said, "Qaf,"*

meaning: I am stopping. He said: In this there is something to consider, because omission in speech only occurs when a proof indicates it, and from where would this be understood from the mention of this letter? End.

﴿And the glorious Qur'an﴾, meaning: possessing glory and nobility over other books.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾

﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾ That is: because a warner of their own kind has come to them, not of the kind of an angel, or from among their own people (jaladah). And it is, as Abu al-Su'ud said, a turning away (idrab) from what is indicated by the answer of the omitted oath (jawab al-qasam), as if it were said: "By the glorious Qur'an, We have sent it down to you so that you may warn the people by it," as occurred at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf. As if it were said after that: "They did not believe in it; they made each of the warner and the thing he warned of an object of denial and wonder, though both are most in accord with the requirements of reason and closest to being received with acceptance."

It has been said: the estimated meaning is: "By the glorious Qur'an, indeed you are a warner." Then it was said after that: "They doubted it," then he turned away from it. It has also been said: ﴿Rather, they wonder﴾ meaning: they were not content with doubt and rejection, but affirmed opposition, to the point that they regarded this as one of the strange matters. It has also been said: it is a turning away from what is understood from describing the Qur'an as glorious, as if it were said: the reason they are not convinced to believe in the Qur'an is not that it has no glory, but rather their ignorance.

﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾ This is an explanation of their wonder, and a statement that it accompanies the extreme of denial, along with further detail regarding the object of their wonder. "This" points to his being, peace and blessings be upon him, a warner with the Qur'an. Their pronoun appearing first (as "they") is to signal that they are specified by what is attributed to them, and their explicit mention second (as "the disbelievers") is to record upon them disbelief in its requirement; or it is a conjunction of their wonder at the resurrection upon their wonder at the prophethood. Moreover, this "This" points to an ambiguous matter which is explained by the following denial-sentence.

the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[3] ﴿When we have died and become dust—that is a far-off return.﴾

﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾ This is an affirmation of wonder and an emphatic denial. The governing element of (idhā) is an implied verb that needs no explanation, because of its well-known status and because of what follows it indicating it: that is, "When we die and become dust, shall we be returned?" as the warner and the one warned speak of it, together with the complete contrast between us and life at that time.

﴿That﴾ refers to the point of dispute. ﴿is a far-off return﴾ meaning: far from imagination, or from custom, or from possibility.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a Book preserved.﴾

﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them﴾ That is: what the earth consumes of their bodies after their death. This is a refutation of their disbelief in it ( istib'ad), and a removal of it. For whoever's knowledge is all-encompassing and so subtle that it reaches the point of knowing what the earth diminishes of the bodies of the dead, consuming their flesh and bones, how could their being returned to life as they were be deemed far-fetched? It was also said: the meaning is what of them dies and is buried in the earth.

﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾ Abu al-Su'ud said: That is, a preserver of the details of all things, or one protected from alteration. What is intended is either a depiction of His knowledge, Exalted is He, of the universals and particulars of things, by the knowledge of one who has a comprehensive Book from which everything is received. Or it is an affirmation of His knowledge, Exalted is He, of them, by their being recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) with Him.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[5] ﴿Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state.﴾

﴿Rather, they denied the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿when it came to them﴾, meaning: without any reflection or contemplation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a second "rather" (idrab) that follows the first, to indicate that they came with something more hideous than their amazement, namely denying the truth, which is prophethood established by miracles, at the very first instant and without reflection or pondering. Its being more hideous lies in the explicit denial without pondering after they had expressed amazement at it.

﴿So they are in a confused state﴾, meaning: disturbed and agitated, referring to the disagreement in their statements about it, such as claiming that it is poetry or sorcery and the like, out of obstinacy and arrogance.

[6] The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and there are no rifts in it?﴾

﴿Have they not looked﴾ — that is, these deniers of the Resurrection, who reject Our power to bring them back to life after their passing away. ﴿At the sky above them, how We constructed it﴾ — that is, We raised it up without pillars. ﴿And adorned it﴾ — that is, with the stars. ﴿And there are no rifts in it﴾ — Ibn Jarir said: meaning, there are no cracks or fissures in it, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You see no imperfection in the creation of the Most Merciful. So return your gaze; do you see any flaw? Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 3–4], that is, exhausted from seeking to see any defect or deficiency.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[7] ﴿And the earth — We spread it out and cast into it firmly set mountains, and We caused to grow therein of every beautiful kind of pair.﴾

﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾ means: We spread it out (basaṭnāhā).

﴿And We cast into it firmly set mountains﴾ means: mountains that are fixed, as a safeguard for it against agitation, because of the strength of the turbulence within its interior (al-jayashān). ﴿And We caused to grow therein of every kind﴾ means: of every sort (ṣinf), ﴿beautiful﴾ means: pleasing to behold, by which one is delighted because of its beauty.

(p-5486)

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[8] ﴿As a insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance.﴾

﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back﴾: that is, so that He makes every servant who turns back, returning to his Lord and reflecting upon the wonders of His creation, see and be reminded.

﴿Insight﴾ (tabsirah) and "reminder" (dhikra) are in the accusative, governed by the last verb, as they are objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), although they are, in meaning, the reasons for the actions mentioned. Or they are governed by an implied verb, meaning: We did what We did as an act of giving insight and giving reminder.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 50, verses 9–11:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[9–10–11] ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water, and We cause to grow thereby gardens and grain of harvest. And the tall palm trees, having spathes of fruit-clusters stacked one upon another.﴾ [Qaf: 10] ﴿As provision for the servants; and We give life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the Emergence.﴾ [Qaf: 11]

﴿And We send down from the sky﴾ i.e., from the clouds, ﴿blessed water﴾ i.e., abundant in benefits. ﴿And We cause to grow thereby gardens﴾ i.e., trees bearing fruit, ﴿and grain of harvest﴾ i.e., the cultivated crop that is harvested, of wheat, barley and all other kinds of grain. The specific mention of the growth of grain is because it is the primary intended purpose.

﴿And the tall palm trees﴾ [Qaf: 10] i.e., and We caused to grow, by the water which We sent down from the sky, palm trees that are tall, or laden (with fruit). It is from (absaqat al-shah), meaning when the ewe became pregnant. Thus it would be of the form (af'ala), so its active participle is (fa'il), whereas the analogical form is (mufil). It is therefore among the rare forms, like (tawa'ih) and (lawaqih), along with other anomalous counterparts. Its separate mention, despite its inclusion in "gardens," is to demonstrate its excellence through the abundance of its benefits. Placing the grain between them serves to emphasize their independence and distinction from the rest, along with the consideration of the rhyme (fawasil).

﴿Having spathes of fruit-clusters stacked one upon another﴾ [Qaf: 10] i.e., layered one on top of another.

﴿As provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf: 11] i.e., for their sustenance. Abu al-Su'ud said: it is a reason (ʿilla) for His saying, ﴿So We cause to grow﴾. In giving this as a reason after the first reason for causing growth, which was insight and admonition, there is an alert that the duty of the servant is that his benefit from this be in terms of remembrance and insight, which is more important than his enjoyment of it in terms of sustenance. It has been said: ﴿provision﴾ [Qaf: 11] is a verbal noun derived from the meaning of "We caused to grow," since growth is provision. ﴿And We give life thereby﴾ [Qaf: 11] i.e., by that water, ﴿to a dead land﴾ [Qaf: 11] i.e., a barren land, which then produced all kinds of plants and flowers.

﴿Thus will be the Emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11] i.e., their emergence alive from the graves. He compared the resurrection and raising of the dead by His power, may He be exalted, to the bringing forth of plants from the earth after the rain falls upon it. So "thus" is the predicate of "the Emergence," or the subject, in which case the kaf carries the meaning of "like."

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[12–14] ﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass (the Well), and Thamud,﴾ ﴿and 'Ad, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot,﴾ [Qaf: 13] ﴿and the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubba'. Each one denied the messengers, so My warning came true.﴾ [Qaf: 14]

﴿Before them﴾, i.e., before Quraysh, ﴿the people of Noah﴾. Abu al-Su'ud said: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to establish the reality of resurrection, by showing that all the messengers, peace be upon them, agreed on it, and by mentioning the punishment of those who denied it.

﴿The companions of the Rass﴾: this is a well by which they lived. It is said they were the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and other things have been said, as was mentioned in Surah al-Furqan.

﴿Thamud﴾: they are the ones who disputed with Salih and killed the she-camel.

﴿'Ad﴾ [Qaf: 13]: they are the ones who disputed with Hud about their idols.

﴿Pharaoh﴾ [Qaf: 13]: he is the one who disputed with Musa concerning what he was sent with. Al-Razi said: He did not say "the people of Pharaoh," because Pharaoh was the one who was arrogant, who made his people feeble-minded, and who was domineering in his affairs.

﴿The brothers of Lot﴾ [Qaf: 13]: they are the ones who disputed with him over approaching men.

﴿The companions of the Thicket﴾ [Qaf: 14], i.e., the thicket of trees, who disputed with Shu'ayb over measure and weight.

﴿The people of Tubba'﴾ [Qaf: 14]: al-Mahayimi said: they disputed with their imam and their scholars in religion. The discussion of this has passed in Surah al-Hijr and al-Dukhan.

﴿Each one denied the messengers﴾ [Qaf: 14], i.e., each of these nations and these generations denied their messenger, (p-٥٤٨٨) and whoever denies one messenger is as if he has denied all the messengers, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105], though only one messenger came to them. Thus, in reality, had all the messengers come to them, they would have denied them. This was conveyed by Ibn Kathir, and it is an explanation for the plural "messengers." The pronoun in "denied" is singular in accordance with the word "each" (kull), which is singular in form though plural in meaning.

﴿So My warning came true﴾ [Qaf: 14], i.e., the threat that He promised to whoever disbelieved became binding upon them, and it is punishment and vengeance. Ibn Jarir said:

Indeed, in this verse, the Exalted described what He described of His descending punishment upon these who denied the messengers, as a warning from Him to the polytheists of Quraysh, and to inform them that if they do not turn back from denying His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), He will bring upon them a punishment like that which He brought upon them. That is, it is a consolation to the Messenger, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, and a threat to them.

﴿The people of Tubba'﴾ [Qaf: 14]: al-Mahayimi said: they disputed with their imam and their scholars in religion. The discussion of this has passed in Surah al-Hijr and al-Dukhan.

﴿Each one denied the messengers﴾ [Qaf: 14], i.e., each of these nations and these generations denied their messenger, (p-٥٤٨٨) and whoever denies one messenger is as if he has denied all the messengers, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105], though only one messenger came to them. Thus, in reality, had all the messengers come to them, they would have denied them. This was conveyed by Ibn Kathir, and it is an explanation for the plural "messengers." The pronoun in "denied" is singular in accordance with the word "each" (kull), which is singular in form though plural in meaning.

﴿So My warning came true﴾ [Qaf: 14], i.e., the threat that He promised to whoever disbelieved became binding upon them, and it is punishment and vengeance. Ibn Jarir said:

Indeed, in this verse, the Exalted described what He described of His descending punishment upon these who denied the messengers, as a warning from Him to the polytheists of Quraysh, and to inform them that if they do not turn back from denying His messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), He will bring upon them a punishment like that which He brought upon them. That is, it is a consolation to the Messenger, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, and a threat to them.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[15] ﴿Did We grow weary with the first creation? Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾

﴿Did We grow weary with the first creation?﴾ That is: Did We become incapable of originating (creation) until We would be incapable of restoring it?! The interrogative particle (hamzah) here is for denial. Al-Shihab said: "Al-ayy (incapacity) here means inability (ajz), not fatigue." Al-Kisa'i said: "You say: u'yītu (I was made weary) from fatigue, and 'ayītu (I was unable) from the cessation of resource and inability regarding a matter." This is the well-known and more eloquent usage, although many do not distinguish between them.

"The first creation" is the origination described above. It may also be understood as the creation of the heavens and the earth, since the creation of man came after it, and the verse supports this: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33], and so on.

His words ﴿Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ are a conjunction with an implied clause, indicated by what precedes it, as if it had been said: "They acknowledge the first creation, so there is no basis for their denial of the second. Rather, the matter has become confused and obscure to them, because they do not grasp the restoration of what has died and whose parts have been scattered, and because they turn away from the authority of divine power and the ease of this for the things decreed by the Lord."

A Subtle Point:

al-Nasir said: "There are three questions concerning the verse: Why did He define 'the first creation,' and indefinite 'confusion' and 'a new creation'?"

Know that definiteness serves no purpose except to magnify and exalt what is intended to be defined. Among its examples is the definiteness of "the males" in His words ﴿And He bestows males upon whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. For this purpose "the first creation" is defined, because the aim is to make it a proof of the possibility of the second creation by a stronger argument: that is, if Exalted God is not wearied by the first creation, despite its greatness, then the later creation is even more fitting not to weary Him. This is the secret of defining "the first creation."

As for indefiniteness, its matter is divided: at times it is intended to magnify the indefinite thing in respect of its vagueness, as if it were too grand to be addressed in a definite form. At other times it is intended to diminish the indefinite thing and belittle it. The first usage is found in ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58], His words ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3], and ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and bliss﴾ [al-Tur: 17], and it is more than can be counted. The second is the basic function of indefiniteness, so it needs no illustration. Thus the indefiniteness of "confusion" is for exaltation and magnification, as if He said: "in confusion of what kind!" The indefiniteness of "a new creation" is to diminish it and make its matter seem slight in comparison with the first creation. It may also be for magnification, as if it were a matter too great for a person to accept being obscure to him, when its soundness is the first thing one perceives in it. End.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[16] ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.﴾

﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ means: what his soul speaks to him, that is, what occurs to the mind. His words, exalted is He, ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ are an illustration of nearness in meaning through a visible, perceptible image. He made this nearness more complete than the furthest degree of physical nearness, in which no joining is closer among bodies, since there is no distance between the part that is joined and that to which it is joined.

Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji, in his gloss on al-Baydawi) said: He used the nearness of the Essence to mean nearness of knowledge, since He is exalted above spatial nearness, either as an illustration or by naming the cause and meaning the effect, because nearness to a thing is normally a cause of knowing it and its states. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, knows his states, hidden and manifest, better than any knower. He gave the example of nearness with the jugular vein because a person's limbs and veins are joined by way of being parts of the whole, so their joining is stronger than the joining of anything that is attached to him from outside. This was singled out because it is the source of his life, and it is within the view of everyone. The word al-habl (the vein) means the vessel; it is likened to one of the ropes (habl, pl. hibal), so its idafah (construction) is either explanatory (bayan) or of the type "the general to the specific" (idafat al-'amm li-l-khass). If the vein is kept in its literal sense, then its construction is like "lujayn al-ma'" (the silver of water, i.e., the water's own kind of thing).

Notice (tanbih):
Ibn Kathir interpreted the verse differently from what preceded, by taking "We" as a reference to the angels. His words are: "That is, His angels are closer to the human being than his jugular vein is to him." He said: "Whoever interprets it as knowledge only does so to avoid implying indwelling (hulul) or unity (ittihad), and both are negated by consensus. Exalted is Allah and sanctified. However, the wording does not require this, for He did not say, 'and I am closer to him,' but said, ﴿and We are closer to him﴾, as He said regarding the dying person: ﴿And We are closer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 85), meaning His angels. And as He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ (al-Hijr: 9). The angels sent down the Reminder, which is the Qur'an, by Allah's permission, mighty and majestic. Likewise the angels are closer to the human being than his jugular vein, by Allah's empowering them, majestic and exalted, to do so. The angel has an influence (lammah) over the human being just as Satan has an influence; for this reason Satan runs through the son of Adam like the blood runs."

Then Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, supported what he had mentioned with what is reported concerning the verse after it. The first interpretation is more precise and closer, and in it there is, along with the warning and the extent of the breadth of knowledge, a definition of the majesty of the divine station, the beauty of which is not hidden.

The interpretation of one who explained it as knowledge is not merely to flee from indwelling and unity, but is for that and for what was mentioned first. Just as preferring "We" over "I" does not settle what it negates, because "We" may be used to express glorification, as is common, so that interpretation is not established by it. Yes! The noble wording may bear what he mentioned, namely that it came as a glorification of the angel, since he acts by Allah's command and permission. But there is no necessity that calls for this, together with the known principle that the literal sense is the default. Allah have mercy on him, by those who understood indwelling and unity he meant someone who said in explaining the verse, like al-Qashani, something of the following sense: "He was closer despite there being no distance between the part joined to it and it, because the joining of a part to a thing testifies to separation and duality, which return to real unity. His accompaniment and nearness to His servant are not like that, for His identity and His reality, which are contained within His identity and His actualization, are not other than Him. Rather, His particular, specific existence is in fact the very reality of His which is existence as such; were it not for Him, it would be pure nonexistence and absolute nothingness." End of al-Qashani's words. Nothing of indwelling or unity in the commonly known sense is understood from this, since these people have a well-known terminology, and they are the first to disavow indwelling and unity, as I have made clear, together with the proof of their impossibility, in the book Dala'il al-Tawhid (Proofs of Divine Oneness), which by Allah's praise was printed in the recent past. So return to it and ask forgiveness for its author.

I say: I then saw Ibn Kathir preceded in this by his teacher, the Imam Ibn Taymiyya, for he clarified this, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book Sharh Hadith al-Nuzul (Commentary on the Hadith of Descent): "There is no description of the Lord, exalted is He, as being near to everything at all in the Qur'an. Rather, the nearness mentioned in the Qur'an is specific, not general, like His words: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ (al-Baqarah: 186). So He, glorified is He, is near to whoever calls upon Him. Likewise what is in the two Sahihs, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that they were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and they were raising their voices with the takbir (Allahu akbar), so he said: 'O people! Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; rather you are calling upon One who is Hearing and Near. Indeed, the One you call upon is closer to one of you than the neck of his mount.' He said: 'Indeed the One you call upon is closer to one of you,' and did not say that He is near to every existing thing. Likewise the saying of Salih, peace be upon him: ﴿Then seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance; indeed my Lord is near and responsive﴾ (Hud: 61). It is known that his words ﴿near and responsive﴾ (Hud: 61) are connected to repentance and seeking forgiveness. He meant by it: near and responsive to the forgiveness of those who seek forgiveness and turn to Him, just as He is Merciful and Loving. Nearness is paired with responsiveness, and it is known that one does not say 'responsive' to every existing thing; responsiveness is only to one who asks Him and calls upon Him. Likewise is His nearness, glorified and exalted is He. The absolute names of Allah, such as His names the Hearing, the Seeing, the Forgiving, the Grateful, the Responsive, and the Near, are not required to relate to every existing thing; rather each name relates to what suits it. His name the All-Knowing, since everything is fit to be known, relates to everything."

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾, what is meant is His nearness to him through the angels. This is what is known from the earlier exegetes of the Salaf (righteous predecessors). They said: "The Angel of Death is nearer to him than his family, but you do not see the angels." Some said: "And We are closer to him" by knowledge, and some of them said: "by knowledge, power, and sight." These statements are weak, for there is nothing in the Book and the Sunnah describing Him with a general nearness to every existing thing, so that they would need to say "by knowledge and power." But some people, when they thought He was described as being near to everything, interpreted that as meaning He knows everything and is capable of everything, as though they supposed that the word "nearness" is like the word "accompaniment." It is established from the Salaf that they said, concerning the verse ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ (al-Hadid: 4), that He is with them by His knowledge while being above His Throne. Ibn Abd al-Barr and others mentioned that this is a consensus of the Companions and the Successors, with no one opposing it.

Then he said: "Nothing like this has come in the wording of nearness, that He said: 'He is above His Throne, and He is near to everything.' Rather He said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ (al-A'raf: 56), and He said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ (al-Baqarah: 186)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated with his chain that "a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Is our Lord near, that we may whisper to Him, or far, that we may call out to Him?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ (al-Baqarah: 186), the verse." It is not said in this context: "near by His knowledge and power," for He knows everything and is capable of everything, and they did not doubt that, nor did they ask about it. They asked only about His nearness to the one who calls upon Him and whispers to Him, so He informed them that He is near and responsive.

Some of the People of the Sunnah interpret nearness in the verse and the hadith as knowledge, since it is the intended meaning: when He knows and hears the supplicant's call, the supplicant's aim is achieved. This is what led those who say He is near to everything in the sense of knowledge and power to say so. This was said by some of the Salaf and many of the later scholars. But none of them said that the very Essence of Him is near to every existing thing. This meaning is affirmed by all Muslims, whether they say He is above the Throne or that He is not above the Throne.

Then he said: "All of these have as their intent that the meaning is not that the Essence of the Creator, exalted is He, is near to the servant's jugular vein and to the dying person. Those who thought the intended meaning was His nearness alone, excluding the angels, explained it as knowledge and power, as in the case of the word 'accompaniment.' But there is no need for this, for the meaning of His words ﴿and We are closer to him than you﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 85) is: through Our angels, in both verses. This is unlike accompaniment, for He did not say 'and We are with him'; rather He made Himself the one who is with the servants, and informed that He will tell them on the Day of Resurrection what they did. He is the very One who created the heavens and the earth, and He is the very One who rose over the Throne. So a word is not to be made like a word when the Qur'an distinguishes between them."

Then he said: "His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ cannot mean mere knowledge, for whoever knows a thing better than others is not called closer to it than others merely by his knowledge of it, nor merely by his power over it. Furthermore, He, glorified is He, knows what is spoken secretly and what is spoken aloud, and He knows their deeds. So there is no meaning in singling out the jugular vein as meaning that He is closer to the servant than it is, for the jugular vein is near the heart, not near the outward speech, while He knows the human being's outward and inward. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ (Ta-Ha: 7). What indicates that nearness does not mean knowledge is the context of the verse, for He said: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾, informing that He knows the whispering of his soul. Then He said: ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾, affirming knowledge and affirming nearness, and making them two different things, so that one is not the other. He restricted the nearness with His words: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾ (Qaf: 17), the verse."

[p. 5495] As for the one who thinks that what is meant by this is the nearness of the Lord's essence to the jugular vein, and that His essence is closer to the dying person than his family, this is extremely weak. Those who say that He is in every place and that He is near to everything in His essence do not single out any one thing over another. No Muslim can say that Allah is near to the dying person and not to his family, or that He is near to the jugular vein and not to the rest of the limbs. How can this statement be valid according to their own principle, since in their view He is in every part of the human body, and He is in the family of the dying person just as He is in the dying person? How could He be closer to him than to you when He is with him and with them in one and the same manner? Could He be closer to Himself than to Himself?

The context of the two verses also shows that what is meant is the angels. He said: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾ [Qaf: 17]. So He restricted the nearness to this time, which is the time of the receiving of the two receivers, namely the two guarding angels who record, as He said: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]. It is well known that if it were the nearness of the essence, He would not have restricted it to this state, and the mention of the two companions, the watcher (al-raqib) and the ready (al-ateed), would have had no fitting meaning.

Likewise is His saying in the other verse: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83-85]. This may be said as follows: if there is someone who could see Him in some states, but we do not see Him, then the Lord, Exalted is He, in this state is not seen by the angels or by humans. Also, He said: ﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85], so He informed about the One who is nearer to the dying person than the people who are with him in this state. As for the essence of the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted is He, if it is said that He is in a place, or it is said that He is near to every existing thing, it is not restricted to this time, place or states, so He would not be nearer to one thing than to another. It is not permissible to mean the particular nearness of the Lord, as in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. That is His nearness to the one who calls upon Him or worships Him. This dying person may be a disbeliever and a wicked one, or a believer who is brought near. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿But if he is of those brought near, then rest and provision and a garden of pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88-89]. ﴿And if he is of the companions of the right, then, peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90-91]. ﴿But if he is of the deniers, the astray, then a welcome of boiling water, and burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92-94]. It is well known that such a denier is not singled out by the Lord with a nearness that excludes those around him, and there may be believing people around him. Rather, they are the angels who attend the believer and the disbeliever, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 97]. And the Exalted said: ﴿If you could but see when the angels take in death those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50]. And He said: ﴿If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming pangs of death, and the angels are extending their hands, [saying], "Expel your souls. Today you are awarded the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth and were, toward His verses, arrogant"﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. The Exalted said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail [in their duty]﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take your souls; then to your Lord you will be returned"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11].

Among what indicates this is that He mentioned it in the plural form, saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. This is like His glorified saying: ﴿We recite to you from the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe﴾ [al-Qasas: 3]. The Exalted said: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 3]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17], ﴿so when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18], ﴿then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19]. When such a term is used by Allah in His Book, it indicates that what is meant is that He, glorified is He, together with His soldiers and helpers from among the angels. The phrase (nahnu) ("We") is said by one who is followed and obeyed, who is honoured and has soldiers who follow his command. No one has soldiers who obey him as the angels obey their Lord, who is their Creator and their Lord. So He, glorified is He, knows what the soul whispers within itself, and His angels know it too. Thus the word (nahnu) here is the fitting one. Likewise is His saying: ﴿And We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf: 16]. He, glorified is He, knows that, and His angels know that, as is established in the two Sahihs from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When the servant intends a good deed, it is recorded for him as one good deed; if he does it, it is recorded for him as ten good deeds. And when he intends an evil deed, it is not recorded against him; if he does it, it is recorded as one evil deed; and if he leaves it for the sake of Allah, it is recorded for him as one good deed." So the angel knows what the servant intends of good and evil, and that is not from the unseen knowledge which Allah has singled out for Himself.

Then he said: His saying: ﴿And We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ implies that He, glorified is He, and His soldiers charged with this, know what the soul whispers to the servant, as He said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes, and Our messengers with them are recording﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80]. So He hears, and whoever of His angels He wills.

As for writing, His messengers record, as He said here: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]. The Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12]. He reported the writing with (nahnu) ("We") because His soldiers write by His command. In that verse He distinguished between hearing and writing, because He hears by Himself.

As for the recording of deeds, it occurs by His command, and the angels write. So His saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him﴾ is like His saying: ﴿And We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12], because His angels draw near to the servant by His command, just as they were recording his deeds by His command. That is His nearness to everyone through the mediation of the angels, just as His speaking to His servant is through the mediation of the messengers. The Exalted said: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by inspiration or from behind a partition or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. So this is His speaking to all His servants through the messengers, and that is His nearness to them at the time of death and at the time of inner and outer speech. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

And the Exalted's saying:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[17] ﴿When the two receivers receive, one sitting on the right and one on the left.﴾

﴿When the two receivers receive, one sitting on the right and one on the left.﴾ That is: We are nearer to man than his jugular vein, at the time when the two angels, the guardians, record what he utters. Here, ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh, "when") is an adverbial clause modifying ﴿أقرب﴾ (aqrab, "nearer"). It contains an indication that He is free of any need for the two angels to guard (the record), for He knows better than they do and is aware of what is hidden from them, but He ordained it for a wisdom that required it: to establish the proof against the one (who is recorded), and to present to the other what encourages and deters him.

Al-Qashani said: Through this verse, Exalted is He clarified His nearness so that nearness in the sense of joining and accompaniment is negated, as the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, said: "He is with every thing, not by accompaniment; for a thing is through Him that thing, and without Him it is not a thing so as to be accompanied." That is: He knows the discourse of the soul, which the self whispers to him at the time of the two receivers' recording, while being nearer to him than they are. Their recording is only for the sake of establishing the proof against him, and for the recording of statements and deeds in the luminous scrolls, for the sake of recompense.

Then he said: The receiver sitting on the right is the rational practical faculty, imprinted with the forms of good deeds and marked by sound, good statements. He sat on the right because the right is the strong, noble, blessed side, the side of the soul that is close to the Truth. The receiver sitting on the left is the imaginative faculty, which is imprinted with the forms of bestial and predatory human deeds, the satanic and illusory opinions, and corrupt, foul statements. He sat on the left because the left is the weak, base, ill-omened side, the side that is close to the body. Moreover, the human nature is good by its essence, being from the world of lights, inclined by its essence and its disposition toward good things. Evils are only accidents that befall it from the side of the body, its organs and its states. The companion of the right dominates the companion of the left. Whenever a good deed proceeds from him, he records it for him at once; but if an evil deed proceeds from him, he restrains the companion of the left from recording it at once, awaiting glorification, that is, purification from the bodily veils and natural states, by returning to its original abode, its true origin and its innate state; so that the effect of that accidental matter is effaced by the original light and by seeking forgiveness, that is, by being illumined with spiritual lights and turning toward the Divine Presence, so that the effect of that accidental darkness is effaced by the light that has come, as has been related: "The recorder of good deeds is on the right of a man, and the recorder of evil deeds is on his left. The recorder of good deeds is trustworthy over the recorder of evil deeds. When he does a good deed, the angel of the right records it as ten; when he does an evil deed, the companion of the right says to the companion of the left: 'Leave it for seven hours; perhaps he will glorify God or seek forgiveness.'" End of quotation.

In the words of al-Qashani, may God have mercy on him, the interpretation of the angel as the faculty urging toward good, and of Satan as the faculty that seduces toward evil, occurs frequently. The philosophers preceded him in this. Some of the philosophers said: "This thing that is deposited in us, which we call faculty and thought, is in reality a meaning whose essence cannot be grasped, and a spirit whose reality cannot be fully known. It is not far-fetched that God Exalted should name it an angel and name its causes angels, or whatever names He wills, for naming is not restricted for people. How then could it be restricted for the One of absolute will, binding authority and all-encompassing knowledge?"

Al-Ghazali had preceded him to this meaning and expressed it by the term "cause." He said, in his explanation of the wonders of the heart in the book of (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), after dividing thoughts into praiseworthy and blameworthy: "Likewise, the light of the heart and its darkness have two different causes: the cause of the thought that calls to good is called an angel, and the cause of the thought that calls to evil is called a satan..." etc. The whole discussion contains gems and is worth consulting.

A subtle point:

﴿قعيد﴾ (qa'id, "sitting") is like ﴿جليس﴾ (jalis) in the sense of ﴿مجالس﴾ (mujalis, "companion"), in wording and meaning. It is used in the singular for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), with the first dropped because the second indicates it, as in the poet's words:

"Indeed, I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

It was also said that the form ﴿فعيل﴾ (fa'il) is applied to both the singular and the plural, as in His words: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporter﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. This was held weak, because it is not applicable in every case; rather, ﴿فعيل﴾ in the sense of ﴿مفعول﴾ (maf'ul) is so only under its conditions, and this (form) is in the sense of ﴿فاعل﴾ (fa'il), so it is not valid here except by way of treating it as ﴿فعيل﴾ in the sense of ﴿مفعول﴾.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[18] ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is a watcher, ready.﴾

﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is a watcher﴾ means: an angel who observes his deeds. ﴿Ready﴾ means: present. When He mentioned their disbelief in the Resurrection and dispelled it by affirming His power and knowledge, He informed them that they would encounter that soon, and He drew attention to its nearness by using the past tense. So He, glorified is He, said:

The commentary on the words of Allah, Exalted is He:

[19] ﴿And the agony of death has come with the truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾

﴿And the agony of death has come﴾ means its intense severity, which bewilders and occupies the senses and stuns the intellect. ﴿with the truth﴾ means with the promised truth and the established matter, which is death itself; so the bāʾ (ba, "with") here expresses accompaniment (mulābasah). Or it means with the promised truth of the matter of the Hereafter, and of reward and punishment, which he had neglected; so the bāʾ is for transitivity (taʿdiyah), meaning: the agony of death brought the reality of the matter into view, with its inner states, and made them manifest to him.

Al-Shihab said: The word "sakrah" (intoxication) has been used metaphorically (istiʿārah) for intensity. The point of resemblance between them is that each of them removes the intellect. The metaphor is therefore an explicit, actual (taṣrīḥiyyah taḥqīqiyyah) one. It is also permissible to liken death to a drink by way of implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah), and attributing intoxication to it is an imaginative device (takhyīl).

﴿That is what you were trying to avoid﴾ means: you were fleeing it. The sentence is understood as having an implied "say" (qawl), meaning: it will be said to him at the time of death, "That matter which you have seen is the very thing from which you were trying to flee during your life, so flight and escape did not benefit you."

Is the thing referred to by "that" the truth or death? Al-Tibi said: If the statement "And the agony of death has come" etc. is connected to His saying "in doubt about a new creation" [Qaf: 15] and what accompanies it, then the thing referred to by "that" is the truth, and the address is to the wicked person, meaning: there has come to you, O wicked one, the truth which you denied. If it is connected to His saying "And We have indeed created man" [Qaf: 16] etc., then the thing referred to is death. The shift of address (iltifat) is present in both interpretations, and the second is the more fitting, because of His saying after it: "And every soul will come with it, a driver and a witness" [Qaf: 21], and its details: "Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever" [Qaf: 24], "And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not distant" [Qaf: 31]. End of quote.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[20–21] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21]

﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ means: the blast of resurrection. ﴿That﴾ means: the blowing ﴿is the Day of the Threat﴾, i.e., the time when the threat is realized, by witnessing what it had sent forward of deeds and what it had left behind.

﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. Ibn Jarir said: that is, a driver who drives it to Allah, and a witness who testifies against it for what it did in the world, whether good or evil. Are these two angels, or one angel combining both attributes, or is the first an angel and the second the soul itself testifying against itself, or is the driver one of its deeds leading it to the place of its recompense and the witness one of its own limbs? These are opinions. Al-Qashani said: that is, a driver from its own deed, and a witness from its own deed; for every person is drawn toward the object of his gaze and what he has chosen by his deed. The inclination that drives him toward that thing arises only from his awareness of that thing and his judgment that it suits him, whether it is a lowly, bodily matter to which his desire impels him and which his imagination entices and strengthens, or a lofty, spiritual matter to which his intellect and spiritual love move him and which his heart and original nature urge him toward. So the knowledge that predominates over him is his driver toward what he knows, and his witness is the dominant inclination within him, and the firmly rooted love in him (p-5502). The deed written in his record testifies against him by its manifestation in the forms of his organs and limbs, and his book speaks against him with the truth, and his limbs (speak) through the states of his organs formed by his deeds. End.

[20–21] ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 21]

﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ means: the blast of resurrection. ﴿That﴾ means: the blowing ﴿is the Day of the Threat﴾, i.e., the time when the threat is realized, by witnessing what it had sent forward of deeds and what it had left behind.
